A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with DAB renamed DAL and its scope expanded. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison; visual inspection resolved extraction problems in v1's plots.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–5 report original synthetic experiments on piecewise stationary and drifting parametric bandits, including a drift-sensitivity experiment.

after.justification: Section 3 reports original synthetic and data-derived benchmark experiments, including kernel bandits and six real-world benchmarks. Section 4.3 also retains the original drift-sensitivity experiment.

M1.justification: The restart, detector, and forced-exploration loop is retained, but v2 adds a substantive kernel-bandit adaptation: exploration actions are selected through a finite covering construction, with a full-action-set fallback for finite kernel experiments (Proposition 4.2, Corollary 4.4, Appendix A.2). This extends the procedure beyond v1's parametric linear-independence construction.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only synthetic linear, generalized linear, and self-concordant bandits. v2 retains these tasks and adds synthetic kernel bandits plus Criteo traffic, Yahoo! R6A click logs, Quandl stocks, Yahoo Finance stocks, Bioliq sensors, and Zozo advertisements, substantially expanding the represented domains and reward structures.

E2.justification: v2 adds WGP-UCB as an evaluated comparator in the kernel-bandit experiments, including the stock benchmarks (Figures 1–2). The existing parametric comparator families—MASTER, WeightUCB, and ADA-OPKB where applicable—remain.

E3.justification: The principal synthetic experiments change dimension from 5 to 10; SCB experiments also change from 50 to 100 actions and action-norm bound L=4 to L=1. DAL's SCB base learner changes from Logistic-UCB-1 to OFUGLB, while MASTER remains described with Logistic-UCB-1. Added benchmarks introduce substantial new construction and evaluation protocols, including cumulative reward for Bioliq and Zozo.

E4.justification: The random-walk drift-radius sensitivity experiment in v1 Section 5.2/Figure 5 is retained in v2 Section 4.3/Figure 3, including the same crossover between DAB/DAL and WeightUCB. No additional ablation or robustness test is introduced; the new benchmark evaluations and input-data visualizations do not test a separate diagnostic question.

E5.justification: The reported averaging count changes from 30 runs in v1 Section 5.1 to 15 independent runs in v2 Section 3.1.1; the new real-world comparisons also use 15 runs. Both versions display variability bands or error bars without specifying their confidence level, and neither introduces significance testing.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the principal parametric result curves under revised settings, adds four kernel-bandit comparison panels in Figure 1, and reports six new data-derived comparisons in Figure 2. These report DAL attaining lower regret or higher cumulative reward than the displayed comparators. They are new or replaced results, rather than evidence of improvement over v1 under identical settings; the drift-radius result is retained.

T1.justification: v2 adds RKHS and information-gain definitions, covering-set propositions and proofs, and a generalized regret theorem and corollary incorporating kernel complexity and exploration-set size. It also replaces v1's explicit finite-time regret decomposition and detailed Appendix A proof with a generalized order bound and the reference-dependent proof sketch in Appendix B.4.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on a feasible, order-optimal black-box algorithm for piecewise stationary parametric bandits. v2 broadens the central applicability and empirical claims to parametric and non-parametric non-stationary bandits and real-world benchmarks, and adds a claim of improving the best kernel-bandit regret bound. The conditional parametric optimality claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation of apparent robustness when change-point separation assumptions fail, arguing that missed short segments incur limited regret (Section 4.2). Its conclusion explicitly identifies missing drift guarantees and dependence on separation assumptions as limitations. The earlier slow-drift/noise interpretation is substantially retained.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the exploration coefficient 0.01, adds detector pseudocode and finite-action guidance, and provides extensive preprocessing, data-access, hardware, and runtime information in Appendix A. It omits v1's explicit MASTER block-parameter setting. Some new documentation conflicts internally: Yahoo! smoothing uses 2000 rounds in Section 3.2 but 100 rounds in Appendix A.3.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through kernel/GP-bandit literature, newer stationary algorithms, and benchmark sources, including works by Chowdhury and Gopalan, Deng et al., Salgia et al., and Lee et al. It also explicitly identifies Huang et al.'s modular MAB work as the closest precursor and presents the main regret theorem as following from that work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contributions, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around DAL and practical non-stationary learning. Experiments now precede theoretical analysis, detector details move to an experimental appendix, and the theoretical appendix is reorganized. This substantially changes the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v1's separate principal experimental figures are consolidated into v2's 16-panel Figure 1, with revised styling and shared legends. v2 adds a six-panel benchmark figure and five data visualizations, redraws the retained sensitivity plot, and relocates and expands Table 1 with kernel rows and a stationary-input regret column. The overall document template also changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for practical applicability beyond v1's exclusively synthetic parametric evaluation through kernel experiments and six diverse data-derived benchmarks. Added preprocessing, resource information, and covering analysis make the expanded scope more assessable. Tradeoffs include fewer reported runs, unmatched SCB base learners, conflicting Yahoo! preprocessing descriptions, and replacement of the detailed regret proof with a sketch. These weaknesses limit verification but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support across application settings.
